name: deer
sources: McKay, John G. More West Highland Tales. Vol. 2. Scottish Anthropological and Folklore Society. Edinburgh: Oliver and Boyd, 1969, 408, 500.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The deer was a symbolic animal for the Celts. They saw the swift woodland herds as the wild form of their own cattle herds. Cattle followed a strong bull, and deer followed a virile stag. The two animals were tied to gods of masculine power, Esus for cattle and Cernunnos for the stag. The doe and the cow ran in parallel, and their goddesses Flidais and Bóand both stood for maternal love and abundance. Deer offspring appear in myth in the story of the transformed Sadb, who gave birth to her son Oisín the bard. Oisín's name still means 'fawn' in Irish. In the Scottish Highlands, giant goddesses tended vast deer herds, and the island of Jura was home to the Seven Big Women who ran with the deer. The shape-shifting Cailleach Beinne Bhric could take the form of a gray deer.

okr.objective: Explores the deer as a Celtic symbol of wild pride and fertility, sacred to gods and to shape-shifters.
key_results: The Celts viewed the deer as the wild counterpart of their cattle herds.
The stag stood for masculine power and linked the gods Esus and Cernunnos.
In the Scottish Highlands giant goddesses tended deer herds on the island of Jura.
The transformed Sadb gave birth to Oisín, whose name means 'fawn'.
